analysis.one_liner: Make chemical makers prove their products are safe for children before they can sell them.
analysis.headline: A 2008 bill to require safety proof for chemicals in commerce was referred to committee and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Kid-Safe Chemicals Act would have flipped the burden of proof in U.S. chemical regulation. Today, under the 1976 Toxic Substances Control Act, chemicals can be sold without any testing, and the EPA has only restricted a handful since the law passed. This bill would require each manufacturer to submit safety data and a CEO-signed certification, test the most dangerous chemicals first (starting with 300), ban chemicals that fail, run biomonitoring to detect chemicals in cord blood, and create a public database of chemical hazards—all with the goal of a fully safety-determined chemical marketplace by 2020. It also preserved states' rights to set stricter rules, encouraged alternatives to animal testing, and would have funded 'green chemistry' research.
analysis.who_benefits: Children (fetuses, infants, kids), pregnant women, workers exposed on the job, and consumers generally, since most chemicals in commerce today have never been tested for toxicity. It would also benefit companies developing safer chemical alternatives, and small/medium manufacturers seeking technical assistance.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each manufacturer to submit health/safety data and a CEO-signed certification that a chemical is safe, or admit data is insufficient, before it can stay on the market
Requires EPA to identify at least 300 high-priority chemicals for safety review within 18 months, and add 200 more per year until all are reviewed
Requires CDC biomonitoring to detect industrial chemicals in human cord blood, and presumes a priority chemical found there fails the safety standard unless the maker proves otherwise
Creates a public internet database of chemical toxicity, use, and exposure data so the public and workers can see what chemicals they're exposed to
Allows EPA to ban or restrict manufacture, import, or sale of any chemical that fails the safety standard, and to restrict a chemical's use in consumer products if home exposure is unsafe
Explicitly preserves states' authority to adopt or enforce chemical regulations stricter than federal rules, rather than preempting state action
Funds safer-alternative ('green chemistry') programs, technical assistance for small manufacturers, and requires alternatives to animal testing where possible

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers bear the direct cost: mandatory safety testing, CEO-signed certifications, updated filings every 3 years, biomonitoring user fees, and the risk of losing market access for any chemical that cannot be proven safe. The bill acknowledges the chemical industry is a major, important part of the U.S. economy.

drawbacks.text: The bill acknowledges the chemical industry is a major part of the U.S. economy, and requiring safety proof for tens of thousands of chemicals on short deadlines could disrupt supply chains, raise costs for manufacturers of everything from plastics to electronics, and trigger job losses and plant closures — the bill requires EPA to evaluate employment effects and lets the President grant national-security or economic-disruption exemptions

Testing every chemical on the market is a massive scientific and administrative task, and deadlines (safety determinations for 300 chemicals by 2012, all chemicals by 2020) may be unrealistic without a large EPA budget expansion the bill does not fully fund

The '1 in 1,000,000' acceptable risk standard for nonthreshold chemicals and 10-fold child-safety margin are extremely strict, and could effectively ban many chemicals that pose real but very small risks, with unclear benefit

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed to fix a widely acknowledged gap: most chemicals in everyday products have never been tested for toxicity, and current law puts the burden on EPA, not industry, to prove harm. The benefit for children's health, worker safety, and consumer right-to-know is large and largely unmeasurable in dollar terms (chronic disease, learning disabilities, cancer clusters). The cost falls on manufacturers — testing, certification, potential market loss — and indirectly on consumers through product prices, though it also protects the chemical industry's long-term legitimacy by replacing a patchwork of state rules and old law. The bill's timelines were ambitious, but the core shift (industry must prove safety, public gets the data) is a genuine public-health improvement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on May 20, 2008, and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day. No further action was taken — it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Sen. Frank Lautenberg (D-NJ) on May 20, 2008.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.
The bill had 6 cosponsors, all Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers came out ahead: the status quo (under which most chemicals in commerce were never tested, and EPA had restricted only a handful) remained in place, since the bill died in committee without a vote. Consumers, workers, and children did not gain the protections the bill would have provided.

sides.party_line_note: All 7 supporters were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote and no senator is recorded as opposing it; no Republican cosponsor is listed.

industries.note: Under current law, chemical makers face no federal requirement to test most chemicals for toxicity before selling them — the bill's finding 3 and finding 7 state EPA had reviewed only ~2% of chemicals in use since 1976 and banned/restricted only 5 substances in 29 years. The bill would have shifted the burden of proof to industry, requiring testing, certifications, biomonitoring fees, and risking market bans. The bill died in committee, so this industry kept the status quo.

industries.industry: Consumer product manufacturers (e.g., plastics, coatings, furniture, electronics)
industries.note: Would face indirect costs if key chemicals in their supply chains were restricted or banned, but also benefit from a clearer, more consistent federal framework than a patchwork of state rules, since the bill preserves states' right to set stricter rules without preempting them.

The bill would have created market incentives, expedited review, public awards, and funded research centers and technical assistance for small and medium manufacturers developing safer alternatives to toxic chemicals.

industries.industry: Laboratories conducting chemical safety testing (including animal testing labs)
industries.note: Mandatory testing requirements would increase demand for safety data; the bill simultaneously requires EPA to promote replacement and reduction of animal testing where possible, shifting the mix of tests performed.
